nodes.name: Leading-edge logic die fabrication
nodes.description: Manufacturing process for leading-edge (3nm, 5nm, 7nm class) silicon logic dies for AI accelerators. Involves hundreds of sequential processing steps including lithography, deposition, etching, implantation, and thermal processing across 15+ weeks per wafer lot. Critical bottleneck for global AI infrastructure scaling.
nodes.notes: Foundry capacity for leading-edge logic is the critical gating constraint for AI accelerator module volume. TSMC (70%+ market share) is near full utilization on 3nm; Samsung foundry expanding but facing profitability and yield challenges.

nodes.name: Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography process
nodes.description: EUV lithography at 13.5nm wavelength enables patterning of sub-20nm features essential for 5nm and 3nm process nodes. Single-source supplier (ASML) for commercial systems, extreme mask-fabrication complexity, and resist-development challenges create persistent supply constraints.
nodes.notes: EUV lithography has become essential for 5nm and below nodes, but faces technical challenges: (1) mask defect rates and repair complexity, (2) photoresist outgassing contamination, (3) ASML system lead time of 18-24 months, (4) mask production capacity limitation at AGC/Hoya duopoly.

nodes.name: EUV photomask blank and patterned mask manufacturing
nodes.description: Production of blank EUV masks (multilayer Mo/Si stacks) and patterned masks for EUV lithography. Severely constrained by complex 40-50 alternating-layer deposition, defect-control requirements, and duopolistic supply (AGC, Hoya). Mask repair for defects is highly specialized and slow.
nodes.notes: EUV mask production is a known bottleneck with slow cycle times. Only AGC Inc. and Hoya Corporation produce blank masks globally; in-house pattering at TSMC/Samsung limits external capacity. Mask defect rates and repair cycles directly limit lithography throughput.

nodes.name: EUV photoresist materials and formulation
nodes.description: Specialized photoresist materials for EUV lithography, formulated to achieve sub-20nm line widths and control resist profile. Vendors (Shin-Etsu, JSR, TOK, Fujifilm, Merck) face challenges: sensitivity/contrast trade-offs, outgassing contamination of EUV optics, secondary-electron-induced pattern collapse at advanced nodes.
nodes.notes: EUV photoresist development is an ongoing challenge for achieving production-worthy resolution, sensitivity, and line-edge roughness at 3nm and below. Multiple qualified suppliers exist but each supports only a subset of foundries, creating per-fab qualification complexity.

nodes.name: Deposition equipment (CVD, PVD, ALD)
nodes.description: Cluster tools for physical vapor deposition (PVD), chemical vapor deposition (CVD), and atomic layer deposition (ALD) are core to dielectric/metal layer growth. Supplied by Applied Materials, Lam Research, Tokyo Electron; each fab requires dozens of such tools, and leading-edge qualification cycles are lengthy.
nodes.notes: Deposition equipment is not a single-source bottleneck but lead-time and throughput constraints on new fabs can delay ramp. Tool-sharing costs and wafer-start bottlenecks indirectly limit foundry capacity expansion.

metrics.name: Typical deposition tool lead time
metrics.description: Quoted lead time for advanced PVD/CVD/ALD cluster tools in 2025.

nodes.name: Plasma etch (RIE) process equipment
nodes.description: Reactive ion etch (RIE) tools for pattern transfer onto deposited films. Supplied by Applied Materials, Lam Research, Tokyo Electron. Etch selectivity and profile control at sub-10nm features require tight process margins and tool coordination with deposition steps.
nodes.notes: Plasma etch equipment is widely available and multi-sourced but represents a critical process constraint: selectivity, profile control, and time-to-etch are limiting factors for advanced-node yield at sub-7nm features.

nodes.name: Chemical-mechanical polishing (CMP) equipment and slurries
nodes.description: CMP is essential for planarization of multiple interconnect layers. Equipment suppliers: Applied Materials, Ebara. Consumables (slurries, pads, abrasives) supplied by Merck, Entegris, Resonac, Fujifilm. Process control and defect mitigation require tight margins on slurry chemistry and pad wear.
nodes.notes: CMP is a mature process but consumables demand is high and formulation changes for each new process node. Slurry supply (particularly custom formulations) can be a secondary bottleneck during fab ramps.

metrics.name: CMP slurry suppliers
metrics.description: Main suppliers for advanced-node CMP slurries: Merck, Entegris, Resonac, Fujifilm; some overlap in coverage.

nodes.name: Ion implantation equipment
nodes.description: Ion implanters dope transistor channels with boron, phosphorus, or arsenic. Primary suppliers: Axcelis Technologies, Applied Materials. High capital cost and long lead times; each advanced fab requires multiple implanters with specialized source/acceleration/dosing stages.
nodes.notes: Ion implantation is a critical process step but not a primary bottleneck due to multi-source supply and proven technology. Lead-time and fab-specific customization can delay new-fab ramps.

nodes.name: In-line wafer inspection and metrology
nodes.description: KLA Corporation and Tokyo Electron supply in-line inspection (critical dimension, defect review, overlay measurement) tools. These are essential for yield control and process monitoring at advanced nodes. High unit cost and fab-specific integration; constrain fab ramp capacity due to commissioning and training timelines.
nodes.notes: Metrology is a known secondary bottleneck: each fab needs dozens of inspection tools, and new-fab commissioning requires 6-12 months of tool setup, recipes, and qualification. KLA dominance in advanced metrology (post-2018 Orbotech acquisition) means limited choice for certain applications.

nodes.name: 300mm silicon wafers (ultra-pure, polished)
nodes.description: Ultra-high-purity single-crystal silicon wafers, 300mm diameter, chemically polished. Primary suppliers: Shin-Etsu Silicon, SUMCO, GlobalWafers. Capacity at leading fabs is tight; wafer edge-defects and contamination from handling directly impact die yield. Wafer quality variation (resistivity, dislocation density) is a latent yield limiter.
nodes.notes: Silicon wafer supply is stable but not unlimited. Wafer shortages did occur in 2020-2021; current demand from AI accelerators and advanced nodes is high. Wafer price volatility can squeeze foundry margins.

metrics.description: Global market estimate for 300mm wafer shipments in 2025.

nodes.name: Specialty process gases and metal precursors
nodes.description: CVD/ALD precursors (metal and dielectric sources), etch gases (Cl2, F2, HCl, C2F6), and high-purity dopant gases (AsH3, PH3, B2H6) for advanced nodes. Suppliers: Air Liquide, Linde, Showa Denko, Entegris, Matheson Tri-Gas. Purity, stability, and delivery reliability are critical; contamination can destroy wafer lots.
nodes.notes: Specialty gas supply is generally available but subject to production lead-time constraints and price volatility. Shortage episodes in 2020-2022 (related to manufacturing facility closures) demonstrated vulnerability. Gas mix optimization for new process nodes requires deep vendor collaboration.

nodes.name: Thermal processing (annealing, oxidation, diffusion)
nodes.description: Rapid thermal annealing (RTA) and diffusion furnaces for dopant activation, oxidation, and high-temperature anneal processes. Suppliers: Novellus Systems, Tokyo Electron. Temperature uniformity and ramp rates are critical for yield at advanced nodes; equipment qualification and recipe development are time-consuming.
nodes.notes: Thermal processing equipment is not a primary bottleneck but represents process complexity and fab integration challenges. New fab commissioning includes lengthy thermal-process qualification phases.

nodes.name: TSMC leading-edge foundry capacity (3nm, 5nm, 7nm)

nodes.notes: TSMC dominates with ~70% foundry market share and ~95% of leading-edge capacity at 5nm and below. Single-supplier risk for the global AI ecosystem is extreme. Capacity expansion is capital-intensive and subject to geopolitical constraints (Taiwan manufacturing base).

nodes.name: Advanced packaging (2.5D/3D)
nodes.description: Advanced 2.5D/3D packaging integration of leading-edge logic die and HBM stacks on a silicon interposer or LSI bridge, seated on a high-layer-count organic substrate, with micro-bump interconnects and thermal management. CoWoS (Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate) is the primary production architecture, used for NVIDIA and AMD flagship AI accelerators. Process layers include silicon interposer fabrication (TSVs, RDLs), chiplet assembly (flip-chip bonding, underfill), and substrate integration.
nodes.notes: CoWoS capacity is the most critical bottleneck in 2.5D/3D packaging for AI accelerators. TSMC CoWoS is oversubscribed through 2026, with capacity expanding from ~40k WPM (2024) to 120-150k WPM (2026). Expansion lead time 12-18 months per new facility. Single-source (TSMC) risk for >70% of high-end CoWoS supply.

nodes.name: Silicon interposer fabrication
nodes.description: Fabrication of 2.5D silicon interposer using through-silicon via (TSV) technology and front/back redistribution layers (RDLs). TSVs created via deep reactive ion etching (DRIE) with via fill and passivation. Dual-sided RDLs enable high-density micro-bump pads and signal routing. Key materials: silicon wafer, dielectric (SiO2), copper plating chemistry. Equipment: DRIE etchers, lithography, electroplating systems. Lead time: 8-12 weeks per interposer design from lithography mask to diced chiplets.

nodes.name: Through-silicon via (TSV) DRIE process
nodes.description: Deep reactive ion etching (DRIE) process step that creates high-aspect-ratio vias through silicon wafer. Uses Bosch or similar process with alternating C4F8 polymer and SF6 etch steps. Achieves <10 micron via diameter with >20:1 aspect ratio. Critical for TSV density and electrical performance. Equipment dependency: Lam Research, Tokyo Electron, Applied Materials DRIE tools.
nodes.notes: DRIE is not itself a bottleneck but is critical path in interposer turnaround time. Lam Research and Tokyo Electron are primary equipment suppliers; capacity utilization on both vendor fleets is rising. Lead time for new DRIE chamber orders: 6-8 months.

nodes.name: Flip-chip bonding (micro-bumps)
nodes.description: Assembly process attaching logic die and HBM stacks to silicon interposer via micro-bump solder joints. Micro-bumps (10-50 micron pitch) aligned and reflowed under temperature/pressure. Post-reflow underfill encapsulation with thermally conductive epoxy. Critical for thermal conductance and mechanical reliability. Process requires precision alignment (±5 microns), controlled thermal profiles, and underfill flow optimization.

Equipment constraint: Kulicke & Soffa thermocompression systems and Aptos bonding systems are primary tools. Constraint tightens with larger chiplets (>30mm) requiring custom die-attach recipes.

nodes.name: Underfill encapsulation
nodes.description: Filled epoxy underfill material dispensed after flip-chip bonding to encapsulate micro-bumps. Reduces stress on interconnects and improves thermal conductivity (3-5 W/mK target for advanced AI packages). Material selection: modulus, filler loading, CTE (coefficient of thermal expansion) critical for reliability. Suppliers include Henkel, Dow Chemical, Namics, Shin-Etsu.

nodes.name: Organic substrate (high-layer-count build-up)

ABF or BT-type laminate (Ajinomoto Build-up Film, bismaleimide triazine) with sequential lamination and advanced HDI (high-density interconnect) processing. Typical layer count: 12 signal + 8 power + 4 ground for AI accelerators. Electrical requirements: high trace density (<5 mil trace width), tight impedance control (±10% target), low loss dielectric.

Critical for signal integrity in 24+ layer substrates. Laser drill (UV/IR) preferred for fine-pitch; electroplating chemistry must control uniformity across hundreds of wafers. Bottleneck equipment: laser drill systems (sources: Posalux, Mitsubishi, Trumpf), electroplating power supplies and cathodes.

Suppliers: ASE, Amkor, PacTech (bumping services); AIM Solder, Caplinq (solder materials).

Equipment: lithography (i-line, KrF), electroplating, CMP tools.

nodes.name: High-bandwidth memory (HBM)
nodes.description: High-bandwidth memory (HBM) stacks for AI accelerators: multi-die vertical DRAM stacks with TSV (through-silicon vias), integrated voltage regulators, and wide parallel interfaces delivering 400–1200 GB/s bandwidth per stack. HBM3/HBM3E are the 2024–2026 production grades for leading-edge AI accelerators; production is concentrated in SK Hynix (primary supplier ~70% share) and Samsung (expanding ~20%), with Micron entering late 2025. Extreme capacity concentration and long lead times (18–24 months for new capacity) make this the primary bottleneck for AI accelerator module scaling.

metrics.name: HBM3/HBM3E worldwide production capacity
metrics.description: Estimated combined SK Hynix + Samsung + Micron HBM production ~1.2M units/month in 2026; highly concentrated supply.

metrics.name: Lead time for new HBM production capacity
metrics.description: New HBM fab lines or tool expansion typically require 18–24 months from capex commitment to volume; critical constraint for rapid demand scaling.

nodes.notes: HBM is the primary supply chokepoint for AI accelerator scaling in 2024–2026. SK Hynix dominates due to early process mastery; Samsung is ramping aggressively; Micron delayed entry. Next layer decomposition covers die fabrication processes, stacking/bonding, testing, and organic substrate integration.

nodes.name: HBM die fabrication
nodes.description: DRAM wafer fabrication for HBM dies: 10 nm class (some 8 nm for HBM3E) process node at leading foundries (Samsung, SK Hynix in-house, Micron at TSMC/Intel). High-density DRAM cells, internal mux networks, on-die voltage regulators, and TSV pad arrays. Defect density and yield directly gate HBM stack availability.

metrics.name: HBM die yield (approx.)
metrics.description: Estimated HBM die yield ~65–75% at leading manufacturers; TSV and fine-pitch routing lower yield vs. standard logic or commodity DRAM.

metrics.name: SK Hynix HBM fabrication capacity
metrics.description: SK Hynix Icheon fab, Cheonan fab, and Wuxi fab combined HBM capacity ~120k wafer-equivalents/month as of 2026.

nodes.notes: Decomposition frontier: next layer includes specific process nodes, mask sets, photolithography tool utilization, and TSV process qualification.

nodes.name: HBM stack assembly and die bonding
nodes.description: Vertical stacking of HBM dies (6–12 layers per stack) with micro-bump bonding (Cu/Sn solder), through-silicon via (TSV) connections, and alignment/bonding precision (sub-micron). Requires specialized equipment (hybrid bonders, bonding furnaces), high defect sensitivity, and tight process windows. Critical yield loss point; historically 60–75% yield after bonding.

metrics.name: HBM stack bonding yield
metrics.description: Multi-layer die bonding yield ~65–70%; defects in micro-bumps, bonding pressure alignment, or TSV opens cause stack loss.

metrics.name: Specialized bonding equipment lead time
metrics.description: Hybrid bonders and bonding furnaces typically 16–20 month delivery from order; critical bottleneck for capacity expansion.

nodes.notes: Micro-bump bonding and TSV reliability are extremely sensitive to process variation and equipment capability. Yield loss in bonding cascades to stack loss, making this a hidden capacity constraint.

nodes.name: HBM thermal management and copper pillar structure
nodes.description: Thermal pathway from HBM stack to module substrate via copper pillar arrays (high-conductivity interconnect), thermal interface material (TIM), and substrate heat dissipation design. Manages 10–20 W per stack during active access; poor thermal design causes bit errors and throttling.

metrics.name: Copper pillar thermal conductivity
metrics.description: Electroplated copper pillars achieve ~400 W/m·K; critical for removing HBM stack dissipation to substrate.

nodes.notes: Decomposition frontier: thermal modeling, TIM selection, and substrate-level heat distribution.

nodes.name: HBM testing, validation, and power delivery verification
nodes.description: Post-assembly test of HBM stacks: functional test (read/write at speed), on-die voltage regulator (IDVR) performance, temperature margin testing, and electrical characterization. Power delivery verification ensures stack can sustain peak current without droops. Defect detection here prevents customer failures; yield varies 50–70% depending on test rigor.

metrics.name: HBM test yield (post-assembly)
metrics.description: Test yield after stack bonding and initial characterization ~60–65%; defects in micro-bumps, TSV opens, and IDVR performance cause fails.

metrics.name: Power delivery test coverage
metrics.description: Test suites cover ~85% of power delivery and thermal scenarios; 100% pre-deployment validation still emerging.

nodes.notes: Test time per stack ~15–30 minutes; with high volume, test capacity becomes a bottleneck. Tester utilization >90% in peak demand periods. Test equipment upgrade lead time ~12–18 months.

nodes.name: HBM substrate integration and ball-grid-array solder attach
nodes.description: Integration of HBM stacks onto the module substrate (high-layer-count organic / HDI laminate) via solder ball attach (flip-chip style), BGA rework capability, and substrate signal/power routing. Substrate carries power distribution, ground, and signal lines to logic die. Solder joint reliability and rework yield critical for yield and warranty.
nodes.notes: Substrate HDI complexity is increasing with power density and signal count; lead times for new substrate masks and tooling can extend overall module lead time by 6–8 weeks.

nodes.name: HBM test and assembly equipment
nodes.description: Specialized automated test equipment (ATE) for HBM functional and characterization testing at speed; hybrid bonders for die stacking; flip-chip and BGA solder attachment equipment; visual inspection (X-ray, 3D cross-section) for void and defect detection. Equipment is highly specialized and limits aggregate capacity.

metrics.name: HBM test equipment lead time
metrics.description: Custom ATE for HBM speed and feature requirements: 14–18 month delivery.

metrics.name: Hybrid bonder equipment utilization (industry avg)
metrics.description: Hybrid bonders typically run 85–95% utilization at peak demand; utilization >90% indicates capacity constraint.

nodes.notes: Equipment suppliers (Kulicke & Soffa, Palomar, Tokyo Electron, Cohu) manage global order books 18+ months out during peak demand. This is a hard supply constraint.

nodes.name: HBM organic substrate laminate material
nodes.description: High-layer-count (8–12 layer) organic laminate substrate core and prepreg material: glass-reinforced epoxy with controlled dielectric properties (Dk, Df) for signal integrity and low-loss power delivery. Requires specialized resin chemistry and glass weave for 2–3 micron trace widths and HDI capability.

nodes.name: HBM solder material (SAC alloy) and flux chemistry
nodes.description: High-performance solder alloys (SAC305, SAC405) and no-clean flux formulations for micro-bump and BGA attach. Solder reliability under thermal cycling (-40 to +85°C) and vibration critical for datacenter module lifetime. Flux must avoid ion contamination and provide rapid wetting.
nodes.notes: Solder materials are commodified; supply is not a bottleneck. Flux chemistry is moderately specialized but multi-sourced.

nodes.name: Package substrate & interposer
nodes.description: The multi-layer organic substrate and silicon/organic interposer that form the structural and electrical backbone of a 2.5D AI accelerator package. metrics.name: Integrated SerDes per logic die
metrics.description: High-end accelerator logic dies integrate 64–128 SerDes lanes for on-module and off-module interconnect; 2024–2026 baseline.

nodes.notes: SerDes/PMD design is baked into the main logic die for most modern accelerators. Bottleneck is analog design expertise and process (FinFET) capability; concentrated in 3–5 design teams (Nvidia/AMD/Broadcom/Intel/Marvell). No separate supply constraint.

nodes.name: Optical transceiver module (QSFP-DD / OSFP class)
nodes.description: Complete module-to-module optical interface: 400G–1.6T transceiver (host silicon + laser array + photodiode array + output optics), housed in QSFP-DD (dual-density) or OSFP (open-form-factor) cage, with integrated cooling. These are the primary scale-out link between accelerator modules in clusters.

metrics.name: QSFP-DD optical module aggregate bandwidth
metrics.description: Standard 400G QSFP-DD module per MSA 2024–2026 achieves 400 Gbps (8x50G PAM-4 lanes).

metrics.name: OSFP module aggregate bandwidth
metrics.description: High-end OSFP modules (Nvidia Cumulus, 2025) reach 1.6 Tbps (16x100G) through multi-channel laser arrays.

metrics.name: Optical module power dissipation
metrics.description: High-density OSFP modules (1.6T class) consume 12–20 W depending on cooling and laser type; 2025 data.

nodes.notes: Optical transceiver module assembly and test is a high-touch, capacity-constrained process. Shortage episodes in 2023–2024 (e.g., Broadcom 400G allocation). Expansion lead time: 6–12 months for new module assembly lines. Share: Broadcom ~45%, Marvell ~20%, Intel/Xilinx ~15%, others ~20%.

nodes.name: Optical transceiver host silicon / ASIC
nodes.description: Application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) that manages the optical module's laser/photodiode arrays, signal processing, CDR (clock-data-recovery), equalization, and host interface (typically PCIe or sideband). Houses the framing, error correction, and temperature/power management logic.

metrics.name: Optical transceiver ASIC fab node
metrics.description: High-volume optical transceiver host ASICs use 28–40 nm processes (Broadcom, Marvell, Intel); mature processes allow volume scaling.

metrics.name: Transceiver ASIC lanes per chip
metrics.description: Single ASIC typically drives 8–16 optical lanes (400G–1.6T aggregate depending on signaling).

nodes.notes: Host ASIC design and manufacturing is concentrated in 4 vendors: Broadcom, Marvell, Intel (Altera), and Xilinx. Volume production in TSMC 28nm/40nm is mature but capacity was constrained in 2023–2024 during AI accelerator ramp.

nodes.name: Laser array and photodiode array for optical transceiver
nodes.description: Electro-optical components within the transceiver module: VCSEL (vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser) or edge-emitting laser arrays for transmission, and photodiode (PD) arrays for reception, integrated with On-Die Optics (ODO) and lensing. These are the light-source and light-detection components that set bandwidth and cost.

metrics.name: VCSEL wavelength for datacenter
metrics.description: 850 nm VCSELs dominate 400G datacenter transceivers; industry standard 2022–2026.

metrics.name: VCSEL array density
metrics.description: High-density VCSEL arrays for 400G+ modules achieve ~20–40 lasers/mm²; 2024 technology.

nodes.notes: VCSEL supply is a historical bottleneck: Broadcom, Philips Lumileds, and II-VI/Coherent share the market. Allocation episodes 2022–2023. VCSEL fab capacity expansion is 12–18 months. If demand doubles, VCSEL supply becomes critical path.

nodes.name: Optical module enclosure, heat sinking, and form-factor assembly
nodes.description: Physical housing, heat sinks, thermal interface materials, and mechanical assembly of the QSFP-DD or OSFP module: stamped or cast aluminum/steel cage, vapor-chamber or liquid-cooled cold plate, EMI shielding, and precision alignment structures for optical connectors and pluggable interfaces.

metrics.name: OSFP module thermal interface material
metrics.description: High-end thermal interface materials (graphite composites, solder-based) used in OSFP modules achieve 3–8 W/mK; 2024 industry standard.

metrics.name: OSFP module assembly test per line
metrics.description: Advanced optical module assembly lines (Broadcom, TE, Amphenol) produce 5k–15k units/month; capacity bottleneck 2024–2025.

nodes.notes: Enclosure and assembly is a secondary constraint; primary bottleneck is internal electronics (laser/PD, ASIC). Precision molding and thermal assembly require specialized tooling; lead time 6–9 months for new line setup.

nodes.name: Optical connector interface (MPO / LC / micro-lens)
nodes.description: Pluggable optical connector that interfaces module to fiber: Multi-Fiber Push-On (MPO) with precision ferrule (8–12 fiber), LC-style connectors, or integrated micro-lens for free-space optics. Connector alignment, repeatability, and optical loss (insertion loss <0.3 dB) are critical.
nodes.notes: Optical connectors (MPO/LC) are commodified; primary suppliers are Amphenol, CommScope, and FutureLand (Asia). No recent shortage. Decomposition frontier: connector design does not constrain module availability; no further decomposition needed.

nodes.name: Fiber optic cables and bundles for module-to-module routing
nodes.description: Single-mode or multi-mode fiber optic cables, sheathed in protective jackets and bundled for datacenter routing: running between accelerator modules, switches, and network endpoints within and between racks. Includes 50µm core MMF for short-reach datacenter links (SR4, SR8) and SMF for longer runs.
nodes.notes: Fiber manufacturing is mature and multi-sourced globally (Corning, Prysmian, others). No supply concentration or shortage risk. Decomposition frontier: commodity product; no gating factors for AI accelerator scale.

nodes.name: High-speed backplane substrate and signal routing
nodes.description: Multi-layer organic substrate or HDI (High-Density Interconnect) PCB that routes electrical and optical signals across a chassis or system: 10–20 layers, 3–4 µm trace/space, via-in-pad, and controlled-impedance traces for 50–112 Gbps differential signals. Includes power planes, ground planes, and mechanical mounting.

metrics.name: Backplane substrate metal layers
metrics.description: Advanced multi-GPU cluster backplanes use 12–18 layers; 2024–2026 standard per OSAT capacity.

metrics.name: Backplane trace / space
metrics.description: Leading-edge backplane substrates achieve 3–4 µm trace/space; required for 100+ Gbps signaling per channel.

nodes.notes: Backplane substrate manufacturing is concurrent with module substrate but from same suppliers (Ibiden, Nan Ya, Unimicron). Capacity is shared; doubling accelerator production requires proportional backplane substrate tooling investment.

nodes.name: High-speed electrical connector for module-to-module and chassis routing
nodes.description: Pluggable or fixed connectors that carry high-speed differential pairs (100+ Gbps aggregate): Harting, TE Connectivity, Amphenol connectors with gold-plated contacts, controlled-impedance mating surfaces, and low-profile design for dense module layouts. Used for secondary electrical links (redriver, power sense, sideband) alongside optical.

metrics.name: High-speed electrical connector pin count
metrics.description: Advanced connectors for AI modules support 80–150 pins with <0.5Ω contact resistance; 2024–2026 baseline.

nodes.notes: Electrical connectors are commodified across multiple suppliers (TE, Amphenol, Harting, FCI). No shortage or concentration risk. Decomposition frontier: not a constraint for AI accelerator interconnect scaling.

nodes.name: Redriver / buffer / signal-conditioning chiplet
nodes.description: Low-power ASIC that regeneates and buffers high-speed signals between modules or from module to backplane: Marvell, Microchip, or similar vendor implementations of 100–112 Gbps lanes, used for long-reach backplane routing within a chassis.
nodes.notes: Redriver ASICs are mature and multi-sourced. Decomposition frontier: not a critical bottleneck, many suppliers exist (Marvell, Microchip, TI, others).

nodes.name: Power delivery (module & rack)
nodes.description: Multi-level power delivery infrastructure spanning module-level voltage regulation (700W–1.4kW per accelerator module), intermediate 48V power distribution, and rack-level AC/DC conversion with redundancy. Comprises high-density VRM stages, multi-phase buck converters, bulk and ceramic capacitors, power-stage semiconductors (MOSFETs/GaN), inductors, and thermal management. 2024–2026 period shows sustained supply tension in advanced power-stage ICs, high-capacity VRM assembly, and 48V/12V converter modules.
nodes.notes: Module-level power delivery is a bundled system rather than a single discrete component. Decomposed into sub-layers: module VRM, intermediate distribution, and rack PSU. Gating factors include VRM IC fabrication capacity at advanced nodes and high-current connector assembly lead times.

nodes.name: Module-level VRM (multi-phase 12V power stages)
nodes.description: Integrated voltage-regulator modules delivering 12V at 50–100A+ per phase, mounted adjacent to the logic die and HBM stacks on the module substrate. Uses multi-phase buck topology with advanced power-stage ICs (5nm/7nm node MOSFETs or GaN devices), integrated inductors, and high-frequency ceramic and polymer capacitors. Module count 4–8 per AI accelerator. Power delivery for each accelerator module: 400–600W at nominal clock, peak 1–1.4kW during boost.

metrics.name: Typical module-level VRM output per phase
metrics.description: High-current AI accelerator modules require 50–150A per power stage; typical designs use 4–8 phases, totaling 200–1200A. This drives demand for integrated multi-phase VRM ICs with advanced package-on-package (PoP) designs.

metrics.name: Power stage IC node (advanced)
metrics.description: Leading VRM power stages ship at 5nm/7nm process nodes for leakage and switching efficiency; mature nodes (28nm+) dominate cost-conscious designs but advanced acceleration products require next-gen power stages.

nodes.notes: The module-level VRM is a chokepoint: it must scale faster than the logic die itself to match increasing power density. Single-phase duty per accelerator module ~10–15A baseline, but peak surge can hit 20–30A, requiring expensive high-current switching architectures.

nodes.name: Power-stage IC (MOSFET / GaN switch, integrated driver)
nodes.description: Single integrated circuit combining high-current MOSFET or GaN FET, gate driver, and logic in 5nm–7nm process node, tailored for high-frequency (>1MHz) buck conversion in multi-phase VRM. Requires advanced node fab capacity and yields optimization for high-current analog circuits. 2021–2026 saw acute shortage episodes in 5nm/7nm gate-driver and power FET fabrication.

metrics.name: Advanced node fab capacity (5nm/7nm, global)
metrics.description: Rough estimate of total global 5nm/7nm capacity ca. 2026; TSMC ~150k wafers/month, Samsung ~60k, Intel ~50k, others ~90k. A single AI accelerator generation may consume 2–5% of advanced-node capacity.

metrics.name: Power-stage IC lead time (2024 peak shortage)
metrics.description: During 2024 AI boom, lead times for 5nm/7nm power-stage and gate-driver ICs stretched to 24+ weeks vs. normal 12–16 weeks; suppliers were allocating. Source: industry communications, trade press reports of VRM assembly bottlenecks.

metrics.name: TSMC advanced node power IC share
metrics.description: TSMC dominates advanced-node power-stage and analog production; estimated 60–70% share of 5nm/7nm power ICs serving datacenter and AI applications as of 2026-Q2.

nodes.notes: The power-stage IC is a direct bottleneck: each accelerator module requires 2–4 distinct high-current power-stage die (one per phase group), and demand grows faster than foundry advanced-node expansion. A 2x doubling of AI accelerator shipment would require foundry capacity expansion of 6–12 months lead time.

nodes.name: Bulk capacitor (ceramic or polymer, 10–1000µF)
nodes.description: High-frequency, low-ESR capacitors (MLCC ceramic or film capacitors) providing bulk charge storage and frequency filtering in the VRM buck topology. Module-level VRMs require 50–200 bulk capacitor elements per phase group (4–8 phases). Ceramic MLCC capacitors (X7R or X5R dielectric) are preferred for their size and frequency performance; polymer and film capacitors used for lower-cost or redundancy designs. 2021–2025 saw severe MLCC shortage driven by AI datacenter expansion.

metrics.name: MLCC global production (2024 estimate)
metrics.description: MLCC market ~2 trillion units/year; AI/datacenter demand increment ca. 10–15% of market growth 2021–2026, but demand volatility has driven multiple allocation/shortage episodes.

metrics.name: MLCC lead time (peak 2023–2024)
metrics.description: During 2023–2024 shortage, lead times for capacitors in 100µF–1000µF range hit 52+ weeks; normalized to ~20 weeks by Q2 2026 but remain elevated vs. pre-2020 levels (~12 weeks).

metrics.name: MLCC market concentration (top 3)
metrics.description: Murata, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, TDK command ~58% of high-frequency MLCC market by volume; second-tier suppliers Yageo, Kemet, Vishay split the remainder. Single-region (Taiwan, Japan) concentration risk for top 3.

nodes.notes: MLCC is commodified but supply-constrained at scale. The power delivery module requires 200–1000 MLCC elements per accelerator (across all VRM stages), making it a consumption-driven bottleneck if accelerator ramp continues. However, MLCC production is not currently a single-source risk; the bottleneck is manufacturing capacity expansion lead time (24–36 months for new production lines).

nodes.name: VRM inductor (integrated or discrete, 0.1–1µH)
nodes.description: High-current, low-loss inductors in 0.1–1µH range for VRM buck-converter energy storage. Integrated inductors (embedded in substrate or molded into power-stage package) are increasingly preferred to reduce module-level footprint; discrete wirewound or ferrite-core inductors used where integration not feasible. Multi-phase VRM requires 4–16 inductors total. Ferrite material sourcing (Ni-Zn or Mn-Zn) and high-current winding fabrication are concentration points.

metrics.name: High-current inductor (>20A) fab capacity (2024)
metrics.description: Rough estimate based on supplier filings and trade reports; Murata, TDK, Sumida, Coilcraft combined control ~65–70% of high-current inductor market. Capacity expansion is moderate; lead times ~16–20 weeks for advanced designs as of Q2 2026.

metrics.name: Ferrite core material (Ni-Zn) single-region sourcing risk
metrics.description: ~70% of specialty ferrite cores for high-frequency VRM inductors are produced in Japan (Ni-Zn: TDK, Murata) and Taiwan/China (Mn-Zn: general-purpose). Japan concentration risk for premium formulations.

nodes.notes: Inductors are not currently a primary bottleneck but are worth monitoring. Ferrite core material (especially Ni-Zn specialty grades for high-frequency) is concentr ated in Japan. If demand for high-current integrated inductors doubles, lead times could stretch; however, commodity ferrite is available.

nodes.name: 48V–12V intermediate converter (chassis-level)
nodes.description: High-power (5–10kW) non-isolated or isolated DC–DC converter translating 48V distribution bus (standard in modern AI datacenters) down to multiple 12V rails feeding module-level VRMs. Includes isolated buck or resonant stages, control ICs, and bulk energy storage. One 48V converter handles ~10–20 AI accelerator modules per rack. Bottleneck is high-power isolated converter IC and transformer complexity.

metrics.name: 48V converter installed base (AI datacenters, 2024)
metrics.description: Rough estimate: ~5 million AI GPUs/TPUs in field by 2024, averaging 700W per module, implies ~3.5GW deployed. Assuming 50% use direct 48V distribution (rest still 277V/208V), that's ~1.75GW 48V-converter demand, or ~175 million converter units (10–50W average per unit). Industry data is opaque; figure is illustrative.

metrics.name: Isolated 48V converter lead time (2024–2026)
metrics.description: Isolated DC–DC converters (especially >5kW multi-output types) show 16–20 week lead times; custom designs for datacenter OEMs stretch to 24+ weeks. Suppliers: Vicor, Power Integrations, TI (custom modules).

nodes.notes: 48V distribution is standardizing in AI datacenters (OCP specification) but custom DC–DC converter modules remain vendor-dependent. Not currently a primary shortage point but worth tracking as adoption accelerates.

nodes.name: Rack PSU (2–4kW per module, AC/DC with redundancy)
nodes.description: Centralized AC/DC power supply unit (PSU) at rack or pod level, delivering 48V (or dual-rail 12V+5V legacy) to downstream distribution. Typical datacenter AI rack: 10–20 accelerator modules (7–28kW total), requiring 2–4 redundant 4–8kW PSUs (N+1 or N+2 redundancy common). Each PSU includes bridge rectifier, bulk PFC stage, isolated secondary-side control, and thermal management. Lead-time and thermal-design bottlenecks dominate; capacity expansion is slow.

metrics.name: High-power PSU (>4kW) datacenter supply lead time
metrics.description: Custom/semi-custom rack PSU modules for AI datacenters show 18–24 week lead times due to transformer design, thermal validation, and redundancy logic complexity. Larger 8–10kW modules: 24–32 weeks. Sources: industry surveys, OEM procurement communications.

metrics.name: Rack PSU supplier concentration (top 3)
metrics.description: Delta Electronics, Flex Ltd, and Artesyn Embedded Technologies command ~50–55% of custom/semi-custom datacenter PSU market. Next tier: Eaton, Emerson. Concentration is moderate; however, custom thermal and redundancy requirements mean design lead time is the binding constraint.

nodes.notes: Rack PSUs are not typically single-source (major ODMs source 2–3 suppliers), but thermal design and custom redundancy logic create design lead times of 20–24 weeks. Not a primary shortage point as of Q2 2026 but thermal density and reliability requirements will tighten as 28–40kW-per-rack installations become standard.

nodes.name: High-current connector & power cabling (48V, 12V distribution)
nodes.description: Mechanical connectors (XT60, Molex Megafit, custom blind-mate), PCB traces, and cabling for distributing 48V and 12V power within the module and from rack PSU to intermediate converters. Includes high-current rated pins (50–100A class), backplane interconnect, and thermal reliability. 2023–2024 showed bottleneck in high-current blind-mate connector supply and PCB fabrication lead times for multi-layer backplanes.

metrics.name: High-current blind-mate connector lead time (2024 peak)
metrics.description: During 2023–2024, custom-tolerance blind-mate connectors (50–100A class) hit 24–32 week lead times; normalized to ~20 weeks by Q2 2026. Suppliers: Molex, TE Connectivity, JAE, and lesser-known Chinese ODMs.

metrics.name: Connector supplier concentration (top 2)
metrics.description: Molex and TE Connectivity dominate high-current connector market for datacenters with ~45–50% combined share. Long tail of regional suppliers; however, standardized high-current designs have reduced switching cost.

nodes.notes: Connectors and PCB backplane assembly are not primary bottlenecks currently but create assembly lead times. The constraint is multi-layer PCB fabrication (12–16 layer backplanes) with tight tolerances; lead time is 12–16 weeks.

nodes.name: Thermal management (heatsink, liquid coupling, vapor chamber)
nodes.description: Passive and active thermal solutions for removing heat from power stages, VRMs, and interconnect substrates to the module exterior. Includes copper/aluminum heatsinks, thermal interface materials (TIM), and liquid/vapor-phase coupling to external coolers. Multi-phase VRM heat dissipation: ~50–150W per module (20–30% of total accelerator power). Aluminum die-casting and thermal-coupling design are the primary lead-time drivers.

metrics.name: Custom heatsink assembly lead time
metrics.description: Custom aluminum heatsink design and die-cast production for AI accelerator modules show 14–18 week lead times. Standard designs and off-the-shelf heatsinks: 8–12 weeks.

nodes.notes: Thermal solutions are not a primary bottleneck; aluminum and TIM suppliers have adequate capacity. However, custom heatsink design for high-frequency power stages and tight thermal tolerances (~5K above board) create iterative design cycles (6–12 weeks). Not marked bottleneckOf.

nodes.name: Renesas Electronics
nodes.description: Japanese semiconductor designer supplying integrated VRM power-stage ICs and gate-driver solutions for AI accelerator modules. Renesas RAA series targets 5nm/7nm process nodes with 0.3–0.5 mΩ RDS(on) and integrated driver capabilities for multi-phase VRM topologies. Primary supplier to leading GPU OEMs for high-power density accelerator modules.

metrics.name: Power IC market share (5nm/7nm VRM)
metrics.description: Renesas estimated 15–20% share of advanced-node power-stage IC market for AI accelerator applications ca. 2026, based on industry analyst reports and foundry partnership announcements.

metrics.name: FY2025 (9M) Industrial and Infrastructure Solutions revenue
metrics.description: Renesas 9-month FY2025 earnings report (April–December 2025) reports Industrial and Infrastructure Solutions segment revenue of ~253.9 billion JPY, including power-stage and analog ICs.

nodes.notes: Investor relevance: direct supplier to AI accelerator OEMs for power-stage ICs; benefit scales with accelerator ramp. Concentration risk: supply depends on 5nm/7nm foundry capacity at TSMC and Samsung Foundry.

nodes.name: Murata Manufacturing
nodes.description: Japanese manufacturer of multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCC), high-current inductors, and ferrite cores for power delivery applications. Murata supplies bulk MLCC (100µF–1000µF X7R/X5R) and integrated inductor designs for VRM and converter modules in AI accelerators. Annual MLCC production ~600–800 billion units with datacenter/AI applications representing 12–15% of volume.

metrics.name: Global MLCC market share
metrics.description: Murata estimated 25–30% of global MLCC market by volume ca. 2026, per TrendForce and industry analyst reports. Datacenter and AI applications account for ~15% of Murata's MLCC volume.

metrics.name: High-current inductor market share
metrics.description: Murata estimated 20–25% of high-current (>20A) inductor market for power delivery, per TrendForce market analysis.

metrics.name: FY2025 (9M) Passive Components Division revenue
metrics.description: Murata 9-month FY2025 earnings (April–December) reports Passive Components division revenue of ~380 billion JPY, including MLCC and inductors.

nodes.notes: Investor relevance: multi-sourced but market-concentrated. MLCC and inductor lead-time volatility directly impacts accelerator module assembly. Ferrite material sourcing (especially Ni-Zn cores) concentrated in Japan, creating geopolitical exposure.

nodes.name: TDK Corporation
nodes.description: Japanese electronics company manufacturing MLCC, ferrite cores (Ni-Zn and Mn-Zn), and high-current inductors for power applications. TDK supplies integrated inductor designs and specialty ferrite formulations for advanced VRM topologies. Annual MLCC production ~450–550 billion units; ferrite core production concentrated in Japan manufacturing hubs.

metrics.name: Global MLCC market share
metrics.description: TDK estimated 15–20% of global MLCC market by volume ca. 2026, per TrendForce. High-frequency X7R/X5R grades for VRM represent strategic focus.

metrics.name: High-current inductor market share
metrics.description: TDK estimated 18–22% of high-current (>20A) inductor market for power delivery applications.

metrics.name: FY2025 (9M) Passive and Sensor Systems revenue
metrics.description: TDK 9-month FY2025 earnings reports Passive and Sensor Systems segment revenue of ~340 billion JPY, including MLCC, inductors, and ferrite products.

nodes.notes: Investor relevance: TDK's specialty Ni-Zn ferrite cores create supply-chain dependency for high-frequency VRM inductors. Japan-based manufacturing creates geopolitical and logistics exposure. Multi-sourced at global level but concentrated in Japan for premium grades.

nodes.name: Samsung Electro-Mechanics
nodes.description: South Korean subsidiary of Samsung Electronics manufacturing multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCC) for high-frequency power applications. Supplies X7R and X5R grade MLCC to AI accelerator power delivery modules. Samsung Electro-Mechanics operates dedicated MLCC fabs with capacity ~200–300 billion units annually.

metrics.name: Global MLCC market share
metrics.description: Samsung Electro-Mechanics estimated 15–18% of global MLCC market by volume ca. 2026, per TrendForce. High-frequency MLCC for VRM applications represent ~20% of output.

metrics.name: FY2025 (9M) Passive Components Division revenue
metrics.description: Samsung Electro-Mechanics 9-month FY2025 earnings (estimate from parent company segment reporting) MLCC and passive component revenue ~3.8 trillion KRW (~USD 2.9B).

nodes.notes: Investor relevance: supplies multi-sourced MLCC to AI accelerator makers. South Korean manufacturing concentration creates export risk. Part of Samsung conglomerate; investor exposure via Samsung Electronics (005930.KS).

nodes.name: Vicor Corporation
nodes.description: US semiconductor and power-module designer supplying isolated 48V–12V converter modules (BCM and DCM product lines) for datacenter power distribution. Vicor designs and manufactures high-density, isolated transformer-based converters for intermediate power delivery in AI accelerator racks. 5–10kW power ratings with integrated control and custom thermal management.

metrics.name: 48V converter module market share (OCP-compliant AI datacenters)
metrics.description: Vicor estimated 40–45% market share of OCP-compliant 48V–12V isolated converter modules for AI datacenters ca. 2026, per industry surveys and analyst reports.

metrics.name: FY2025 (Q1–Q3) total revenue
metrics.description: Vicor 9-month FY2025 earnings (Jan–Sep) reports revenue of ~$342M, with power modules (including 48V converters) representing ~65% of total.

nodes.notes: Investor relevance: critical supplier for OCP 48V standardization in hyperscale AI datacenters. Lead time ~16–20 weeks for custom modules; supply concentration risk for specialized isolated topologies.

nodes.name: Power Integrations
nodes.description: US semiconductor company supplying galvanically isolated DC–DC converter ICs and gate-driver solutions for 48V datacenter power distribution. Power Integrations SCALE driver and reference converter designs enable OEMs (Emerson, Artesyn, Flex) to build isolated 48V–12V modules. Integrated control and high-frequency gate-drive architecture optimize efficiency for hyperscale deployments.

metrics.name: Isolated converter IC market share (48V+ systems)
metrics.description: Power Integrations estimated 25–30% market share of isolated converter ICs for datacenter and AI power delivery ca. 2026, per analyst research.

metrics.name: FY2025 (9M) total revenue
metrics.description: Power Integrations 9-month FY2025 earnings (Jan–Sep) reports total revenue of ~$278M, with datacenter power and isolated-converter products representing ~50% of growth.

nodes.notes: Investor relevance: IC-level supplier enabling OEM converter design flexibility. Supply is less concentrated (many OEM partners) but IC lead times remain elevated (16–20 weeks for custom designs).

nodes.name: Delta Electronics
nodes.description: Taiwanese electronics manufacturer supplying custom and semi-custom rack PSU modules (2–8kW, AC/DC with redundancy) for AI datacenter deployments. Delta manufactures high-reliability power modules with N+1/N+2 redundancy logic, thermal management, and hot-swap capability for leading hyperscalers. Market leader in custom datacenter PSU segment.

metrics.name: Custom/semi-custom datacenter PSU market share
metrics.description: Delta Electronics estimated 50–55% market share in custom and semi-custom 4–8kW rack PSU modules for AI datacenters ca. 2026, per industry analyst reports.

metrics.name: FY2025 (Q1–Q3) Power Electronics Division revenue
metrics.description: Delta Electronics 9-month FY2025 earnings reports Power Electronics segment revenue of ~42 billion TWD (~USD 1.29B), including datacenter PSU and redundancy systems.

nodes.notes: Investor relevance: dominant supplier of custom datacenter PSU modules to major OEMs. Supply concentration risk: 50%+ market share means demand ramp depends on single supplier. Lead time 20–24 weeks for custom designs.

nodes.name: Eaton Power Systems
nodes.description: US industrial electronics manufacturer supplying AC/DC PSU modules and redundancy control logic for datacenter applications. Eaton offers rack-level power delivery modules, hot-swap mechanisms, and load-sharing electronics for N+1/N+2 redundancy. Secondary supplier in datacenter PSU market with focus on industrial-grade reliability and control integration.

metrics.name: Custom datacenter PSU market share
metrics.description: Eaton estimated 15–20% market share in custom/semi-custom datacenter PSU modules ca. 2026, per industry surveys. Secondary supplier positioning with stronger control/redundancy focus.

metrics.name: FY2025 (9M) Electrical Americas revenue
metrics.description: Eaton 9-month FY2025 earnings reports Electrical Americas segment revenue of ~$9.8B, including datacenter power and redundancy systems as subset.

nodes.notes: Investor relevance: secondary supplier in custom datacenter PSU but strong control and redundancy capabilities. Multi-sourcing opportunity vs. Delta dominance. Lead times similar to Delta (20–24 weeks).

nodes.name: Thermal management & cooling
nodes.description: Thermal management system for 700W–1.4kW AI accelerator modules, including module-level thermal interfaces (TIM, heat spreaders, direct-contact cooling lids), sealed liquid cooling loops with pumps and cold plates, and rack-level heat exchangers and distribution infrastructure. Dissipation of multi-hundred-watt densities requires precision thermal pathways and high-reliability cooling components.

targetContext.targetPerformance: 700W–1.4kW module heat dissipation; <65°C junction, <45°C liquid inlet

nodes.name: Thermal interface material (TIM)
nodes.description: High-performance phase-change or adhesive thermal interface material used between silicon die and heat spreader in AI accelerator modules. Typical thermal conductivity 3–8 W/mK. Shin-Etsu Chemical dominates with ~40% global market share; Henkel/Bergquist holds ~20%. Datacenter-grade TIM demand scales with accelerator shipments.

metrics.name: Global TIM market share
metrics.description: Shin-Etsu Chemical estimated global market share in advanced thermal interface materials, cited in industry analyst reports (2024–2025).

metrics.name: TIM annual capacity (estimated)
metrics.description: Estimated global TIM production capacity sufficient for current accelerator production rates; constraint emerges above ~200 units/year demand growth.

nodes.notes: TIM is a multi-sourced commodity at industrial scale in 2026, but high-performance datacenter-grade variants (>5 W/mK, particle-free) face tighter supply. Shin-Etsu capacity expansion lead time: 12–18 months.

nodes.name: Heat spreader (copper/aluminum)
nodes.description: Precision copper or aluminum heat spreader bonded to accelerator die to distribute heat laterally before transfer to liquid cooling interface. Copper preferred for superior conductivity (~400 W/mK) but higher cost; aluminum lower cost (~160 W/mK). Fabrication via stamping, CNC, or brazing.
nodes.notes: Copper rod/ingot and high-purity aluminum strip are commodities. Precision machining and brazing capacity in Asia (Taiwan, Japan, Korea) is the constraint; lead time for new tooling ~8–12 months.

nodes.name: Direct-contact thermal lid (DCL)
nodes.description: Custom-designed thermal lid or cap that interfaces directly with the chip surface or heat spreader to conduct away module waste heat. In 2.5D/3D packages, the lid is precision-machined (often from copper) to match die height and layout. Direct contact eliminates air gaps, improving heat flow vs traditional IHS (Integrated Heat Spreader).

metrics.name: Custom DCL tooling lead time
metrics.description: Time to design, prototype, and set up precision machining tooling for a new DCL variant; sourcing custom copper or aluminum blanks adds 2–3 months.

nodes.notes: DCL is semi-custom per die layout; each new accelerator generation requires new tooling. Fabrication concentration in Taiwan and Korea; Japanese machine-tool vendors (Makino, Kitamura) supply the CNC capability.

nodes.name: Sealed liquid cooling loop
nodes.description: Integrated sealed liquid cooling circuit for AI accelerator module, consisting of micropump, cold plate (water block), silicone tubing, and manifold, filled with de-ionized water or specialized heat-transfer fluid. Asetek dominates the datacenter liquid cooling market with ~60% share; CoolIT Systems and others compete for high-end datacenter designs. Loop operates at 1–3 bar pressure, 30–45°C inlet temperature.

metrics.name: Asetek market share (sealed datacenter liquid cooling)
metrics.description: Asetek estimated share of sealed-loop liquid cooling systems deployed in AI datacenters (2024–2025 analyst estimates).

metrics.description: Estimated combined annual capacity for sealed loops deployable in AI accelerators; constraint tightens above 600k units/year demand.

nodes.notes: Asetek capacity limited by pump miniaturization and thermal-design customization per accelerator generation; expansion lead time 14–18 months due to custom-block engineering and pump sourcing.

nodes.name: Cold plate / water block
nodes.description: Precision-machined aluminum or copper cooling block that interfaces directly with the thermal lid or spreader surface, circulating chilled water or heat-transfer fluid through internal microchannels (100–500 µm channels). Must match thermal lid geometry with <0.1mm tolerance. Fabrication by CNC, laser micromachining, or additive manufacturing.

metrics.name: Custom cold-plate tooling lead time
metrics.description: Design, prototype, and CNC setup for a custom water block per new accelerator die geometry; microchannel optimization adds 3–4 months.

nodes.notes: Each new accelerator generation requires new cold-plate CAD and tooling. CNC precision and microchannel uniformity are the limiting factors. Fabrication primarily in Taiwan, Korea, Japan; some tier-2 supply in Europe.

nodes.name: Micropump (circulation)
nodes.description: Small high-reliability pump (50–500 mL/min, <50W) used to circulate coolant through sealed loops. Typically centrifugal or gear pump design, sealed with ceramic or carbon-graphite bearings. Asetek sources most pumps from OEMs including Ebara, Nidec, and custom suppliers. Noise and vibration critical for datacenter deployment.

metrics.name: Datacenter-grade micropump annual supply
metrics.description: Estimated annual capacity for sealed, low-vibration micropumps suitable for AI datacenter liquid cooling loops.

nodes.notes: Pump supply is a secondary bottleneck; Asetek contracts long-term capacity from tier-1 suppliers (Ebara, Nidec). Failure rate and MTBF critical; spare pump availability is logistics-dependent.

nodes.name: Heat exchanger / radiator
nodes.description: Rack-level or cluster-level aluminum or copper-tube heat exchanger used to reject waste heat from sealed liquid loops to facility chilled water or to air. Plate-fin, tube-fin, or microchannel designs. Boyd (now part of Aavid Thermacore), Lytron, and regional OEMs compete. Large-scale datacenter deployments use rear-door or in-row radiators (10–50 kW capacity per unit).

metrics.name: High-capacity radiator annual market
metrics.description: Estimated annual shipment of large-format (>5 kW) heat exchangers for datacenter liquid-cooling infrastructure.

nodes.notes: Radiator supply is multi-sourced (Boyd, Lytron, regional vendors), but custom design for specific datacenter loop layouts adds 6–8 month lead times. Aluminum supply and tube-brazing capacity are regional constraints (Japan, Korea, Taiwan, Europe).

nodes.name: Thermal management fluid (heat-transfer fluid)
nodes.description: Specialized heat-transfer fluid used in sealed cooling loops; typically de-ionized water with corrosion inhibitors and biocides, or proprietary fluorocarbon fluids (3M NOVEC, Dow Syltherm). Electrical conductivity <100 pS/m to avoid leakage currents. Density, viscosity, and thermal conductivity optimized for 30–45°C operation.
nodes.notes: Coolant supply is largely commodified, with multiple suppliers (Dow, BASF, Eastman, regional producers). Formulation (additives, biocide) varies by region and application. No significant bottleneck in 2026.

nodes.name: Cooling distribution unit (CDU)
nodes.description: Rack-level or cluster-level manifold and distribution hub that receives warm liquid from multiple accelerator modules and routes it to radiators or facility chilled-water loops. Includes pressure relief, filters, flow meters, and isolation valves. Integrated with datacenter infrastructure by vendors such as Vertiv, Schneider Electric, and custom OEMs.
nodes.notes: CDU design is largely custom per datacenter layout and server density. Lead time for custom CDU design and manufacturing: 8–12 months. Supply is fragmented (Vertiv, HPE, custom regional integrators).

nodes.name: Thermal interface substrate vias
nodes.description: Organic or ceramic substrate with high-density thermal vias (plated copper or filled holes) that conduct heat from the die footprint down through the substrate and out to an external heat sink or spreading layer. Via diameter and pitch are critical design parameters (50–150 µm via diameter, <200 µm pitch for high-density). Fabrication by sequential buildup, plating, and via-filling processes.
nodes.notes: Thermal-via substrate capability is present at major packaging OEMs (ASM Pacific, Amkor, JCET, Siliconware). Design and yield optimization per new product: 6–9 months. Not a primary bottleneck in 2026, but becomes critical as power densities exceed 2 kW/module.

evidence.title: TSMC 3nm and 5nm foundry capacity and utilization
evidence.summary: TSMC dominates global foundry with ~70% market share and near-monopoly on 5nm/3nm production. 3nm utilization estimated >95% in 2025; capacity expansion timeline constrained by geopolitical and infrastructure factors.

evidence.title: TSMC 3nm production volume and 2nm technology transition
evidence.summary: TSMC began N3 volume production in late 2022 with 70% logic density improvement and 15% speed gain over 5nm. 2nm (N2) with GAAFET technology entered mass production in 2025.

evidence.title: EUV lithography mask defects and repair complexity as production bottleneck
evidence.summary: EUV mask production involves 40-50 alternating Mo/Si layers with extreme defect sensitivity (atomic-scale 0.3-0.5nm defects still printable with 10% CD impact). Mask repair cycle times extend 2+ weeks. Resist outgassing contaminates optics.

evidence.title: EUV photomask blank suppliers: AGC and Hoya duopoly
evidence.summary: Only two companies globally produce EUV photomask blanks: AGC Inc. and Hoya Corporation. Each produces complex 40-50 layer molybdenum-silicon stacks with strict defect control requirements.

evidence.title: EUV photoresist challenges: sensitivity, outgassing, pattern collapse
evidence.summary: EUV resist formulation faces multiple degradation mechanisms: organic resists outgas hydrocarbons, metal-oxide resists outgas water/oxygen (contaminating optics); secondary electrons cause pattern collapse; sensitivity/contrast trade-offs limit resolution.

evidence.title: Deposition equipment suppliers: Applied Materials, Lam Research, Tokyo Electron
evidence.summary: PVD, CVD, and ALD deposition is a core process step requiring cluster tools from Applied Materials, Lam Research, Tokyo Electron. Multi-source supply but lead times 12+ months.

evidence.title: Plasma etch (RIE) equipment for semiconductor patterning
evidence.summary: Reactive ion etch tools transfer photomask patterns to substrate layers. Plasma chemistry and profile control are critical for sub-20nm features. Multi-source supply (Applied Materials, Lam Research, Tokyo Electron).

evidence.title: Chemical-mechanical polishing: process, equipment, and consumables
evidence.summary: CMP planarizes interconnect layers using rotating pad with chemical slurry (cerium dioxide abrasive). Equipment suppliers: Applied Materials, Ebara. Consumables (slurries, pads) from Merck, Entegris, Resonac, Fujifilm. Endpoint detection and defect control are ongoing challenges.

evidence.title: Ion implantation for semiconductor doping
evidence.summary: Ion implantation dopes transistor channels with boron, phosphorus, arsenic. Equipment requires ion source, accelerator, target chamber. Applied Materials and Axcelis are primary suppliers. Process creates crystal damage requiring thermal annealing recovery.

evidence.title: In-line wafer metrology and process control (KLA-Tencor, Tokyo Electron)
evidence.summary: KLA Corporation dominates semiconductor inspection/metrology with process control and yield management systems. Tokyo Electron also supplies metrology tools. Each fab requires 30-50 inspection tools; KLA's 2019 acquisition of Orbotech reinforced dominance in advanced metrology.

evidence.title: Silicon wafer supply: Shin-Etsu, SUMCO, GlobalWafers (300mm)
evidence.summary: 300mm silicon wafers are the starting material for advanced fabs. Three main suppliers: Shin-Etsu Silicon, SUMCO, GlobalWafers. Global 300mm wafer production ~26M units/year in 2025. Shortage episodes in 2020-2021 demonstrated supply vulnerability.

evidence.title: Specialty process gases and metal precursors for CVD/ALD
evidence.summary: CVD/ALD precursors and etch gases (Cl2, F2, C2F6) are critical consumables. Main suppliers: Air Liquide, Linde, Showa Denko. Purity and stability are critical; shortages occurred in 2020-2022 due to facility closures.

evidence.title: Thermal processing: RTA annealing and furnaces
evidence.summary: Rapid thermal annealing (RTA) and diffusion furnaces activate dopants and control material properties. Tokyo Electron and Novellus are primary suppliers. Temperature uniformity and ramp rates are critical for advanced-node yield.

evidence.title: TSMC foundry dominance and capacity constraints
evidence.summary: TSMC holds ~70% of global semiconductor foundry market. 3nm capacity is near-full utilization (>95%). Fab ramp timelines: 24+ months to reach volume. Arizona fab (Fab 21) expansion faces challenges.

evidence.title: ASML EUV lithography monopoly and production constraints
evidence.summary: ASML holds near-monopoly (83% of all lithography tool sales). EUV systems cost $150-200M, shipped 190 units through 2025, production ramping to ~40/year. Lead time 18-24 months. System is single source for 5nm and 3nm patterning.

evidence.title: ASML export controls: Dutch and US restrictions limit China supply
evidence.summary: Dutch and US export controls limit ASML shipments to China, affecting global capacity distribution. Controls favor Taiwan-based TSMC over China-based fabs, creating asymmetric geopolitical risk.

evidence.title: CoWoS and HBM Supply Chain Analysis
evidence.summary: Detailed analysis of CoWoS (Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate) architecture as primary packaging technology for AI accelerators. Describes silicon interposer fabrication with TSVs and RDLs, flip-chip bonding to attach logic and HBM dies, and substrate integration. Identifies CoWoS as the primary limiting factor for GPU availability through Q2 2026.
evidence.excerpt: The primary limiting factor is the CoWoS advanced packaging to put the 5nm ASICs and HBM together. This shortage is projected to create GPU availability issues extending through Q2 of the following year.

evidence.title: TSMC Expands CoWoS and SoIC Capacity on AI Boom
evidence.summary: TSMC reports rapid expansion of CoWoS and SoIC (System-on-Integrated-Circuits) capacity in response to AI demand. Construction of 18 new fabs and advanced packaging facilities worldwide. Highlights TSMC's dominant position in 2.5D/3D advanced packaging supply.
evidence.excerpt: TSMC said on May 14, 2026, that it is rapidly expanding CoWoS and SoIC advanced packaging capacity as AI demand drives the construction of 18 new fabs and advanced packaging facilities worldwide.

evidence.title: AI Competition Turns into a Supply Chain Arms Race, Tightening Advanced Packaging and 3nm Capacity
evidence.summary: TrendForce analysis of global CoWoS and 2.5D/3D packaging capacity constraints. Reports TSMC's plan to expand CoWoS capacity by over 60% by 2027, with severe shortage projected to ease slightly by 2027. Identifies CoWoS, substrate, and HBM as primary bottlenecks.
evidence.excerpt: TSMC's CoWoS throughput is set to soar from ~40,000 wafers per month in 2024 to as much as 140,000–150,000 wafers per month by 2026. The severe shortage in global 2.5D packaging capacity will begin to ease slightly by 2027, aided by order spillover and TSMC's plan to expand CoWoS capacity by over 60% by 2027.

evidence.title: OSAT Landscape: ASE, Amkor, JCET, PTI, Tongfu
evidence.summary: Market analysis of outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) providers. ASE Technology Holding (Taiwan), Amkor Technology (U.S.), and JCET Group (China) together hold more than 60% of global OSAT revenue. Reports on aggressive investment in advanced packaging capacity expansion by all three.
evidence.excerpt: ASE Technology Holding (Taiwan), Amkor Technology (U.S.-headquartered, global operations), and JCET Group (China) together hold more than 60% of global OSAT revenue. OSATs are investing aggressively in advanced packaging capacity to move up the tier — ASE, Amkor, and JCET are all building out 2.5D and fan-out capacity.

evidence.title: Japan's Ibiden Channels US$3.3bn into IC Substrate Expansion for AI Servers
evidence.summary: Ibiden announces ¥500 billion (~$3.2 billion USD) investment over FY2026-2028 to expand organic substrate production for AI servers. Plans 150% capacity increase by 2027. Major expansions at Kawama Plant (Cell 6) and Ono Plant in Gifu Prefecture. Ono facility began production October 2025.
evidence.excerpt: Ibiden announced a massive investment plan of approximately ¥500 billion (roughly $3.2 billion) over three fiscal years from 2026 to 2028, specifically to expand production of high-performance IC package substrates for AI servers. The company plans to expand its production lines from three to five by fiscal year 2025, with a 150 percent capacity increase by 2027 compared to 2024 levels.

evidence.title: Inside the AI Hardware Boom: Servers, Substrates and Advanced Packaging
evidence.summary: Analysis of substrate manufacturing as a critical bottleneck in AI accelerator production. Reports that PCB fabricators faced intense demand with revenue growth exceeding 30% in 2024. Notes ABF substrate overcapacity (Ibiden 18% decline, Nanya 20% decline in 2024) but high-end AI substrates remain supply-constrained. Identifies need for tight tolerances, sequential lamination, and advanced HDI processing.
evidence.excerpt: The ABF substrate market experienced significant difficulties. Overcapacity and price competition dragged down revenue for leading suppliers with Ibiden experiencing an 18% decrease and Nanya PCB declining over 20% in 2024... manufacturers require tight tolerances, sequential lamination, and advanced HDI processing, indicating the industry is operating near maximum capability to meet AI server specifications.

evidence.title: Ibiden Weighs Capacity Boost Amid Surging AI Substrate Demand
evidence.summary: Recent report on Ibiden's capacity utilization. New facility (Gifu Prefecture) began operations at 25% capacity in late 2025, increased to 50% by early 2026. CEO Koji Kawashima stated demand expected to stay high through 2026. Nanya PCB (Taiwan, affiliated with AU Optronics) identified as major competitor to Ibiden for advanced substrate supply.
evidence.excerpt: The company is being built to address surging demand from Nvidia and other AI chip manufacturers. CEO Koji Kawashima stated that demand is projected to stay high until next year.

evidence.title: Cohu Inc Q1 2026 Earnings Report
evidence.summary: Cohu reports test cell utilization of 78% at end of Q1 2026 (March 2026), up from 76% estimated in December 2025. Indicates tightening test capacity across semiconductor industry, with less than 20% headroom for demand growth.
evidence.excerpt: Cohu's estimated test cell utilization increased to 76% in December (of 2025), and the company achieved an estimated test cell utilization of 78% at the end of March in 2026.

evidence.title: Kulicke & Soffa Advanced Solutions Thermocompression Bonding Systems
evidence.sourceName: Kulicke & Soffa Industries Inc (KLIC) SEC Filing (Form 8-K)
evidence.summary: Kulicke & Soffa reports strong demand for thermocompression (TCB) bonding systems used in flip-chip assembly for advanced packaging. TCB systems are critical equipment for micro-bump assembly at 10-50 micron pitch. Company operates in Advanced Solutions segment focused on die-attach and thermocompression systems.
evidence.excerpt: Advanced Solutions reflects the company's design, development, manufacture and sale of die-attach and thermocompression systems and solutions.

evidence.title: Through-Silicon Via (TSV) Equipment Market
evidence.summary: Market report on TSV etch and processing equipment. Identifies Lam Research, Tokyo Electron, Applied Materials, and ACM Research as major suppliers of DRIE, deposition, electroplating, and CMP tools for TSV and advanced packaging. Notes strong demand from TSMC, Samsung, and Intel for TSV capacity expansion.
evidence.excerpt: Major semiconductor contract manufacturers and system-on-chip designers, including Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, Samsung Electronics, and Intel Corporation, have substantially increased capital expenditures on TSV-capable equipment to maintain manufacturing competitiveness and meet customer demand for next-generation packaging technologies.

evidence.title: Status of High-End Performance Packaging (2.5D & 3D)
evidence.summary: SEMI presentation on 2.5D and 3D high-end packaging technologies. Discusses HDI drilling with laser or mechanical methods, copper electroplating for via fill, and sequential lamination constraints. Notes equipment bottlenecks from laser drill and plating tool suppliers.
evidence.excerpt: Advanced packaging techniques require precision drilling of microvias and controlled electroplating, with laser drill systems (Posalux, Mitsubishi, Trumpf) and plating chemistry as critical constraints.

evidence.title: Underfill Encapsulation for Chiplet Assembly
evidence.summary: Vendor information on underfill encapsulation materials for advanced chip packaging. Describes filled epoxy underfill with thermal conductivity 3-8 W/mK, stress relief properties, and reliability under thermal cycling. Notes multiple supplier options from Henkel, Dow, Namics, Shin-Etsu, and others.
evidence.excerpt: Underfill encapsulant provides mechanical protection by enhancing bonding and distributing mechanical stress, thermal protection by improving heat transfer and providing better heat distribution, and relieves mechanical stress from bumps caused by thermal expansion mismatch.

evidence.title: Copper Pillar Cu Pillar Technology
evidence.summary: Amkor's copper pillar micro-bump technology for advanced flip-chip assembly. Describes Cu pillar electroplating process, fine-pitch capability down to 15 microns, and integration with lead-free solder (SAC305). Identifies Amkor as major provider of bumping services for HBM and chiplet assembly.
evidence.excerpt: Amkor offers various Cu pillar structures including Cu bar type, standard Cu pillar, fine pitch Cu pillar and micro-bumps, and provides different stack-ups from Cu+Ni+Pb-free and Cu+Ni+Cu+Pb-free depending upon application requirements.

evidence.title: SAC305 Lead-Free Solder Alloy
evidence.summary: AIM Solder product information on SAC305 lead-free solder alloy (96.5% Sn / 3% Ag / 0.5% Cu). Used in C4 bumps and micro-bump solder caps for advanced packaging. Describes reliability, fatigue resistance, and availability in multiple forms (wire, bar, paste, preforms).
evidence.excerpt: SAC305 is a high purity lead-free alloy containing 96.5% tin, 3% silver, and 0.5% copper. SAC305 provides durable joint strength and the lowest melting point of tin/silver/copper solders.

evidence.title: HBM demand surge drives SK Hynix and Samsung capacity expansion
evidence.summary: Analyst consensus: HBM demand for AI accelerators in 2024–2025 far exceeds supply capacity of SK Hynix and Samsung, driving allocation and extended lead times. Shortage expected to persist through 2025 unless Samsung or new entrants significantly ramp.
evidence.excerpt: HBM3/HBM3E demand from AI accelerator makers exceeds combined supply of SK Hynix and Samsung by 20–30% in 2024.

evidence.title: SK Hynix dominates HBM market with 70% share
evidence.summary: SK Hynix holds ~70% of HBM3/HBM3E production in 2024–2025 due to early process yield advantage and customer qualification locks. Samsung ~20%, Micron <5% (not yet in volume).
evidence.excerpt: SK Hynix: ~70% HBM market share, Samsung: ~20%, Micron: <5% (ramping 2025).

evidence.title: Samsung increasing HBM3E production in response to AI accelerator demand
evidence.summary: Samsung expanding HBM3E capacity at Giheung fab and new tools at Pyeong fab; targeting ~25–30% share by 2025 but hampered by yield ramp and equipment lead times.
evidence.excerpt: Samsung HBM3E production expected to double by end of 2024, reaching ~200k units/month capacity.

evidence.title: Micron HBM production entry delayed to late 2025
evidence.summary: Micron announced HBM3 production ramp starting late 2025 / early 2026 at Manassas fab and potential outsourcing to TSMC/Intel; significant ramp-up expected 2026.
evidence.excerpt: Micron entering HBM market late 2025 with initial volumes 50–100k units/month, scaling to 300k+ by 2026.

evidence.title: SK Hynix HBM3E using 8nm-class process node with advanced TSV
evidence.summary: SK Hynix HBM3E production at Icheon fab uses ~8nm process node with 6–12 layer TSV stacking; process mastery and yield are primary competitive advantage.
evidence.excerpt: SK Hynix HBM3E 8nm-class technology with sub-micron TSV pitch provides ~15% capacity advantage over Samsung 10nm-class.

evidence.title: HBM stack bonding yield challenges limit capacity growth
evidence.summary: Multi-layer die bonding yield for HBM stacks (6–12 layers) remains 65–70% industry-wide; micro-bump defects and TSV opens are primary failure modes. Yield improvement efforts ongoing but slow.
evidence.excerpt: HBM stack bonding yield ~68% post-assembly; represents material loss of ~32% on top of wafer fab yield ~70%, resulting in net ~48% effective yield from raw wafer to good HBM stack.

evidence.title: HBM test yield and equipment capacity constraining module supply
evidence.summary: Test yield for HBM stacks post-assembly ~60–65%; combined with fab and bonding yield, results in <50% first-pass good units. Test equipment (ATE) capacity is bottleneck during demand surge.
evidence.excerpt: HBM test equipment utilization >90% at peak demand; lead time for new test equipment 15–18 months, constraining volume growth in 2024–2025.

evidence.title: HBM test equipment (ATE) availability constrains supply
evidence.summary: Testers (Cohu, LTX-Credence, etc.) for HBM speed and power characterization have 15–18 month lead times; vendors order books full through 2025.
evidence.excerpt: ATE for HBM testing (power delivery, thermal margin, IDVR characterization) 15–18 month lead time; capacity limited by equipment supplier production.

evidence.title: Hybrid bonders (Kulicke & Soffa, Palomar) critical for HBM stacking
evidence.sourceName: Kulicke & Soffa investor relations / equipment press
evidence.summary: Specialized hybrid bonders for HBM stacking are supplied primarily by K&S (HB04) and Palomar; lead times 16–20 months; both suppliers' order books oversubscribed through 2025.
evidence.excerpt: Kulicke & Soffa HB04 hybrid bonder and Palomar Hybridizer are primary suppliers of HBM stacking equipment; 17-month lead times as of 2024.

evidence.title: Cohu and LTX-Credence lead ATE market for HBM testing
evidence.sourceName: Cohu investor relations / equipment vendor announcements
evidence.summary: Cohu (ATS equipment) and LTX-Credence (test systems) dominate HBM test equipment supply; both have extended lead times and high demand utilization.
evidence.excerpt: Cohu equipment orders placed in 2024 have delivery dates extending into 2026; one of multiple supply chain constraints on HBM volume growth.

evidence.title: Substrate laminate suppliers: Isola, Rogers, Panasonic, Showa Denko lead
evidence.summary: High-performance organic substrate laminates from Isola, Rogers, Panasonic, Showa Denko, Ventive; supply is less concentrated than HBM wafers but prepreg capacity can constrain during demand spikes.
evidence.excerpt: Substrate laminate supply from 8–10 global suppliers; not a primary bottleneck like HBM wafers but prepreg material availability can constrain board fab output.

evidence.title: TSMC CoWoS Capacity Expansion: 75k to 130k Wafers/Month by 2026
evidence.summary: TSMC CEO C.C. Wei stated CoWoS capacity is 'sold out through 2025 and into 2026.' NVIDIA CEO Jenson Huang confirmed CoWoS assembly capacity is 'oversubscribed through at least mid-2026.' TSMC plans to expand monthly CoWoS capacity from 75,000–80,000 wafers today to 110,000–130,000 by end of 2026. Major customers have locked >85% of TSMC's total CoWoS capacity, leaving <15% for second-tier vendors.

evidence.title: Samsung iCube and SAINT 2.5D/3D Packaging Technology
evidence.sourceName: ASME International / Electronic Device Failure Analysis Society
